title: A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation
research_question: How can online supervised learning systems characterize, detect, adapt to, and evaluate changes in the relationship between inputs and targets over evolving data streams?
methodology: This is a comprehensive survey rather than a new controlled experiment. It organizes concept-drift research into an adaptive-learning framework containing memory, change detection, learning, and loss-estimation components, and reviews representative algorithms within those categories. It also analyzes forgetting strategies, fixed and variable windows, explicit drift detectors, adaptation mechanisms, and evaluation procedures for time-ordered data. The survey discusses application examples and proposes evaluation criteria for both predictive performance and change-detection quality.

key_findings.finding: Concept drift includes changes in the target distribution conditional on observed inputs, and changing user interests in a news stream are presented as a canonical example.
Adaptive learning can be decomposed into memory, change detection, learning, and loss-estimation modules, allowing different adaptation strategies to be combined modularly.
Shorter recent-data windows react faster to changes but can be less stable, whereas larger windows improve stability in stationary periods while adapting more slowly.
Recency alone is not a reliable proxy for relevance when data are noisy or concepts recur, so simple window-based forgetting can discard useful older information.
Explicit change detection provides information about when and how a process changes beyond the implicit adaptation obtained from continuously updating an online model.
Drift detectors should be evaluated not only by downstream predictive accuracy but also by true-change detection, false alarms, detection delay, and change-point localization accuracy.
Ordinary randomized cross-validation is inappropriate for evolving streams because it destroys temporal order; holdout and prequential test-then-train procedures are presented as alternatives.

limitations: The survey focuses primarily on online supervised learning where labels or delayed feedback are available, not on unsupervised semantic state tracking in workplace communication.
As a 2014 survey, it cannot cover later developments in drift detection, continual learning, modern recommender systems, or language-model-based personalization.
The work synthesizes heterogeneous prior algorithms rather than conducting a uniform empirical benchmark across all reviewed methods.
Many drift-handling techniques assume a stream of labeled instances and do not directly specify symbolic work-item transitions such as new, open, resolved, or superseded.
The survey does not address briefing-specific omission, repetition, evidence attribution, or obligation-versus-preference ranking.
raw_claims: Concept drift occurs when the data-generating relationship changes over time.
A user's evolving interest in incoming news is an example of real concept drift.
Adaptive models may update continuously or retrain on recent batches.
Adaptive-learning systems can be understood through memory, change detection, learning, and loss-estimation components.
Fixed and variable sliding windows are common ways to emphasize recent data.
Small windows favor reactivity while large windows favor stability.
Recency-based forgetting can fail when concepts recur or observations are noisy.
Explicit drift detectors can identify change points or intervals of change.
Change detection should be assessed for missed changes, false alarms, delay, and localization error.
Temporal ordering must be preserved when evaluating adaptive stream learners.
Prequential evaluation tests each new observation before using it for learning.
